source_text: Nam si non imputat iustitia, nisi unde liberum est abstinere; et ante Baptisma necessitas mali est, quoniam voluntas, sicut dixisti, ad faciendum bonum non est libera, perque hoc aliud agere non potest nisi malum; ab infamia mali ipsa quam patitur necessitate defenditur; quoniam apud eam iustitiam gravari operibus suis non potest, quae non imputat malum, nisi a quo liberum est abstinere. Post Baptisma autem, si necessitas boni est, nullum utique potest esse peccatum. Vide igitur quam illud quod esse peccatum ratio demonstrat, inveniri nequeat in seminibus, quando secundum definitiones tuas iam nec in moribus invenitur.
pass_a_gloss: For if justice does not impute, except from where it is free to abstain; and before Baptism there is a necessity of evil, since the will, as you said, is not free toward doing good, and through this cannot drive another thing except evil; it is defended from the infamy of evil by the necessity itself which it suffers; since before that justice it cannot be weighed down by its own works, which does not impute evil, except from which it is free to abstain. But after Baptism, if there is a necessity of good, there can at any rate be no sin. See therefore how that which reason demonstrates to be sin cannot be found in seeds, when according to your definitions it is already not even found in manners.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice

pass_b_english: For if justice imputes only what one is free to abstain from, and before baptism there is a necessity of evil, since the will, as you said, is not free to do good and consequently can do nothing but evil, then the very necessity it suffers defends it against the disgrace of evil. It cannot be burdened with its deeds before that justice which imputes no evil except what one is free to abstain from. After baptism, however, if there is a necessity of good, there certainly cannot be any sin. See, then, how impossible it is to find in seed what reason shows sin to be, when according to your definitions it can no longer be found even in conduct.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
